Table 3. Pre- and post-treatment scores of psychosocial functioning of depressed children treated with cognitive-behavioural treatment (CBT, N = 29) and non-focused intervention (NFI, N = 28)
Cognitive-behavioural treatment (CBT) appears to have considerable value in the treatment of childhood depression.
[/page/2/Text/4] As part of a controlled trial of cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) for children and adolescents with depressive disorders, we devised a formal treatment protocol:
[/page/2/Text/6] CBT is described in detail in Vostanis and Harrington (1994).

three main treatment components thus are: recognition and labelling of emotions; enhancement of social skills; and changing negative cognitive attributions. The CBT did not directly target co-morbid psychiatric disorders or family difficulties, although it was anticipated that there might be indirect effects (Kendall, 1994).

[/page/3/Text/15] The child is encouraged to develop further his or her ability to pay attention and observe his or her own thoughts and feelings. The aims and content are similar to those of the first session, although the child is now encouraged to make some judgements about potential causal links between mood, events and thoughts. [/page/3/Text/24] The child is encouraged to engage further in social activities and thus enhance self-esteem. More detailed discussion, including role play, focuses on specific social and interpersonal difficulties. Self-reinforcement may be used to encourage desirable activities. [/page/3/Text/26] The child is facilitated to distinguish between internal and external effects on mood and is asked to give examples of cognitions and events that usually precipitate depressed mood. Negative thoughts are then challenged by asking the child to provide 'evidence' that these are justified.
[/page/4/Text/6] The CBT was piloted in a clinical setting for one year, and it was revised several times until a detailed treatment manual was developed.
[/page/5/Table/4] Treatment Cognitive-behavioural N = 29
At the end of treatment, 25 CBT subjects (87 percent) and 21 controls (75 percent) did not present any longer with a depressive disorder.
Table 3. Pre- and post-treatment scores of psychosocial functioning of depressed children treated with cognitive-behavioural treatment (CBT, N = 29) and non-focused intervention (NFI, N = 28)

[/page/9/Text/3] Meanwhile we recommend the use of cognitive-behavioural treatment for depressed children and adolescents, with an early introduction of self-monitoring, social problem-solving and cognitive restructuring.
